title: Early Developmental Pathways to Autism and ADHD in Infancy: A Survey of Mechanisms, Markers, and Emerging Clinical Implications

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations: Infant Development as a Framework for Emerging Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
Normative developmental trajectories in infancy are characterized by rapid but uneven change across motor, attentional, perceptual, and social-communicative systems. A central developmental principle is that early competencies are probabilistic rather than fixed, with later outcomes emerging through dynamic reorganization rather than simple linear growth. Longitudinal work in developmental psychopathology has emphasized that continuity and discontinuity can coexist: early variation may be transient for some children, while for others it marks the beginning of increasingly stable patterns of adaptation or maladaptation ref [1].

Against this background, atypical trajectories relevant to autism and ADHD are best understood as divergences from expected developmental timing, sequencing, or integration, rather than as the mere early presence of later diagnostic symptoms. Prospective infant-sibling studies of autism have shown that behavioral signs are often subtle or absent in the first months, with clearer social-communication and attentional differences emerging over the second year of life ref [2], ref [3]. Similarly, developmental models of ADHD suggest that early risks may be visible in temperamental regulation, activity level, and emerging executive control, but these features show marked heterogeneity in onset, stability, and clinical significance across children ref [4].

A trajectory-based perspective therefore shifts emphasis from single early markers to patterns of change over time. This approach is especially important because equifinality and multifinality are common: similar early vulnerabilities can lead to different outcomes, and similar later phenotypes can arise from different developmental routes ref [1], ref [5]. Mapping both normative variation and atypical divergence in infancy provides the conceptual foundation for identifying when, how, and for whom emerging neurodevelopmental differences consolidate into autism, ADHD, or related profiles.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations: Infant Development as a Framework for Emerging Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
A developmental psychopathology perspective treats autism and ADHD not as static entities but as outcomes of dynamic developmental processes unfolding across time. Classic formulations emphasize that adaptation and maladaptation arise through transactions among biological liabilities, behavior, and context, and that the same early vulnerability can lead to different later outcomes depending on developmental timing and environmental contingencies ref [6], ref [7]. This framework is therefore especially useful in infancy, when symptoms are not yet fully organized into diagnostic syndromes but early differences in attention, regulation, social engagement, and motor development may begin to alter subsequent developmental pathways.

Two principles are particularly relevant for emerging neurodevelopmental disorders: multifinality and equifinality. Early social-communicative atypicalities, temperamental dysregulation, or attentional control difficulties may precede autism, ADHD, both conditions, or neither, illustrating that common early risks can diverge into distinct outcomes; conversely, similar later phenotypes can arise from different combinations of genetic, neural, and experiential influences ref [7], ref [8]. Developmental psychopathology also highlights continuity and reorganization: early traits may show homotypic continuity, but they can also be transformed as children encounter new cognitive and social demands, making infancy a period of risk expression rather than diagnostic finality.

This perspective aligns closely with current neurodevelopmental research that seeks mechanisms rather than fixed categories. Cicchetti and Toth argued that understanding psychopathology requires integrating normative developmental processes with atypical pathways ref [9], while Sonuga-Barke and Halperin proposed that ADHD is best understood developmentally, in terms of cascading interactions among early neuropsychological vulnerabilities and environmental inputs ref [10]. Applied to autism and ADHD, developmental psychopathology thus encourages prospective, longitudinal, and transdiagnostic models that explain how early perturbations become stabilized, compensated, or amplified over development.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations: Infant Development as a Framework for Emerging Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
A central debate in developmental research on autism and ADHD concerns whether these conditions are best understood as discrete diagnostic categories or as the extreme end of continuously distributed traits. Dimensional models are especially compatible with infancy research because variation in attention, social communication, sensory responsivity, and activity level is observable long before stable clinical diagnoses are assigned. Population and family studies indicate that autistic traits and ADHD-related behaviors are continuously distributed, with clinical cases differing quantitatively more than qualitatively from subthreshold presentations ref [11], ref [12].

For autism, evidence from epidemiologic and psychometric work has supported a continuum model in which social-communication differences and restricted or repetitive behaviors extend into the general population, even while categorical diagnoses remain clinically useful for service allocation and prognostic communication ref [11], ref [13]. Parallel arguments have been made for ADHD, where taxometric and latent-variable studies have generally favored dimensional over natural-class accounts of inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive traits ref [14], ref [15]. From a developmental perspective, dimensional models better capture heterogeneity, changing symptom expression across age, and the accumulation of risk across multiple domains.

At the same time, dimensional and categorical approaches need not be treated as mutually exclusive. Contemporary frameworks such as the hierarchical taxonomy of psychopathology emphasize dimensional liability structures, while allowing clinically meaningful thresholds and cross-disorder co-occurrence to be modeled explicitly ref [16]. In infant studies, this integration is particularly valuable: early variation may index probabilistic developmental pathways, whereas later categorical outcomes reflect contingent interactions among traits, environments, and clinical decision rules.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations: Infant Development as a Framework for Emerging Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
Autism and ADHD can be understood as partially overlapping developmental outcomes that arise from both shared liabilities and syndrome-specific pathways. Population and family studies indicate substantial co-occurrence and shared genetic influences, challenging models that treat the conditions as wholly independent categories ref [17], ref [18]. From an infant-development perspective, this implies that early differences in attention control, arousal regulation, social orienting, and motor development may represent transdiagnostic liabilities whose later expression depends on timing, severity, and interactions with the environment.

Prospective infant-sibling studies support this view by showing that early behavioral markers are often not diagnosis-specific. For example, elevated familial likelihood for autism is associated with broad alterations in attention, motor functioning, and social communication before diagnostic consolidation, with different combinations of early features predicting later autism, ADHD traits, or broader developmental difficulties ref [19], ref [20]. Such findings are consistent with developmental cascades in which initial perturbations in one domain reorganize functioning in others over time.

At the same time, distinctions remain important. Comparative work suggests that autism is more consistently linked to early differences in social attention and communicative reciprocity, whereas ADHD is more closely associated with later-emerging difficulties in activity regulation, inhibitory control, and sustained attention, even though these domains can interact from infancy onward ref [21], ref [22]. A developmental framework therefore emphasizes both equifinality and multifinality: similar early vulnerabilities may lead to different outcomes, while similar clinical phenotypes may arise through different developmental routes.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations: Infant Development as a Framework for Emerging Neurodevelopmental Disorders
subsections.content:
Transactional and ecological models emphasize that infant development is shaped through continuous, reciprocal exchanges between the child and the multiple environments in which development is embedded. Sameroff’s transactional framework argues that biological characteristics and caregiving contexts mutually influence one another over time, such that early vulnerabilities are amplified, buffered, or redirected through ongoing interaction ref [23]. Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological model similarly situates development within nested systems—from proximal family routines to broader social and structural conditions—highlighting why early manifestations of autism- and ADHD-related traits cannot be understood as properties of the child alone ref [24].

In this view, neurodevelopmental risk emerges through dynamic coupling between infant regulatory style, attention, sensory responsivity, parent-infant interaction, and contextual stressors. Developmental psychopathology has therefore stressed probabilistic pathways rather than linear causation, with adaptation reflecting transactions across levels of analysis and across time ref [25]. For infants who later show autistic or ADHD-related features, caregiver responsiveness, sleep and feeding challenges, family adversity, and access to supportive environments may alter developmental cascades, affecting the consolidation of social communication, executive control, and emotion regulation.

An ecological-transactional perspective also helps explain heterogeneity and uneven developmental timing. Early differences may change meaning depending on environmental fit, cumulative exposure, and compensatory processes, consistent with models of experiential canalization and developmental cascades ref [26], ref [27]. This framework therefore supports longitudinal, multilevel research designs that integrate infant behavior with family, community, and societal contexts when characterizing pathways to later neurodevelopmental outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Neurocognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Alterations in social attention are among the most intensively studied infant markers of later neurodevelopmental divergence. In prospective studies of infants at familial likelihood for autism, reduced orientation to faces, eye contact, and socially contingent cues has been observed during the first year, although effects are often subtle and developmentally dynamic rather than uniformly present from birth. A particularly influential longitudinal analysis suggested that declining attention to eyes across early infancy, rather than a static deficit, may characterize infants later diagnosed with autism ref [28]. Experimental work using direct gaze and social engagement paradigms similarly indicates that diminished attention to socially relevant stimuli can emerge before clear behavioral symptoms are clinically evident ref [29].

Early communication differences often co-occur with these attentional atypicalities. Lower rates of responding to name, reduced reciprocal vocal–affective exchange, and delays in joint attention behaviors have repeatedly distinguished infants who later show autism-related outcomes from both low-risk peers and high-risk infants without later diagnosis ref [30], ref [31]. Joint attention is especially important because it links emerging social orienting with later language and social learning; impairments in initiating or responding to shared attention cues may therefore index a broader disruption in social information processing ref [31].

At the same time, heterogeneity is substantial. Some infants later diagnosed with autism show age-appropriate early social interest, and social-communicative markers may interact with general attentional control and developmental level. Related work on infant siblings has also highlighted atypical face scanning and reduced preference for biological motion, suggesting that early communication risk may reflect multiple partially independent pathways within social perception and engagement systems ref [32], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Neurocognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Attention regulation in infancy is a prominent candidate marker because it sits at the interface of perceptual selection, state control, and emerging executive function. Prospective studies of infants at elevated familial likelihood for autism have reported atypical trajectories in visual orienting, disengagement, and the allocation of attention across social and nonsocial events, suggesting that early differences may reflect domain-general control processes rather than only social-specific atypicalities ref [34], ref [35]. Related work has argued that infant attention skills provide building blocks for later executive capacities, including inhibitory control and flexible shifting, making them especially relevant for transdiagnostic risk models spanning autism, ADHD, and broader developmental difficulties ref [36].

Among the most replicated findings is slower attentional disengagement in some infants who later show elevated autistic traits or receive an autism diagnosis. In a longitudinal infant-sibling design, Elsabbagh and colleagues found prolonged disengagement from central stimuli at 6 to 10 months in infants later meeting criteria for autism, supporting the view that early control of gaze and orienting may be an informative precursor ref [37]. However, group differences are heterogeneous, and not all high-risk infants show the same profile, indicating that attentional regulation is best understood as one probabilistic component within a broader developmental cascade.

Executive precursors are also visible in early patterns of sustained attention, effortful state regulation, and emerging inhibitory processes. A developmental framework proposed by Johnson, Posner, and Rothbart links infant orienting and alerting systems to later executive attention, highlighting plausible mechanisms through which early attentional atypicalities could shape learning opportunities and downstream self-regulation ref [36]. In parallel, atypical attention in the first year has been implicated in later ADHD-related pathways, including elevated activity and poorer regulation, reinforcing the value of infancy attention measures for parsing shared and distinct developmental liabilities ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Neurocognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Motor development has emerged as a prominent candidate early marker because postural control, spontaneous movement, and the organization of goal-directed action are measurable in the first year and are closely coupled with later social-communicative learning. In prospective infant-sibling studies, infants later diagnosed with autism often show lower fine and gross motor skills by the end of the first year, with delays sometimes evident before clear social symptoms are clinically recognized ref [39]. Broader reviews likewise suggest that motor atypicalities are among the earliest and most replicated developmental differences associated with autism, although they are not specific to autism and may also index more general neurodevelopmental liability ref [40].

Evidence from home-video and prospective studies further indicates that qualitative features of action may be informative alongside milestone timing. Reduced movement variation, atypical postures, and differences in anticipatory or object-directed actions have been reported in infants who later develop autism ref [41]. In high-risk infant cohorts, early fine-motor delays also predict later expressive language and social-communication outcomes, supporting the view that motor development may shape opportunities for exploration, joint engagement, and learning rather than merely co-occur with later symptoms ref [42].

At the same time, motor markers should be interpreted cautiously. Similar early motor delays can be observed in infants who later show ADHD-related difficulties or other developmental challenges, limiting diagnostic specificity. Nonetheless, because motor behavior can be assessed repeatedly, often objectively, and prior to robust symptom expression, it remains a valuable component of multivariate early identification models, particularly when integrated with social, attentional, and sensory indicators ref [40], ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Neurocognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Atypical sensory processing is among the most frequently reported early features in infants who later show elevated likelihood of autism or other neurodevelopmental difficulties. Prospective infant-sibling studies indicate that differences can be detected within the first year, including heightened or reduced reactivity to visual, auditory, and tactile input, as well as unusual patterns of sensory seeking or aversion. These early sensory features are of interest not only because they may precede clearer social-communication symptoms, but also because they may shape infants’ opportunities for learning and engagement with caregivers and the environment ref [44], ref [45].

Longitudinal work suggests that sensory hyperreactivity and hyporeactivity in infancy are associated with later autism-related outcomes and broader functional difficulties. In high-risk cohorts, parent-reported sensory behaviors at 12–18 months have been linked to later ASD symptom severity and adaptive functioning, supporting the view that sensory atypicalities may represent an important developmental pathway rather than a peripheral correlate ref [45], ref [46]. Converging evidence from observational and caregiver-report studies further shows that elevated sensory over-responsivity can co-occur with difficulties in attention, affect regulation, and social orienting, underscoring the cross-domain significance of early sensory regulation ref [47].

At the same time, sensory markers are not specific to autism and likely index transdiagnostic liability. Dimensional frameworks emphasizing sensory reactivity across neurodevelopmental conditions are therefore useful, particularly given overlap with later ADHD symptoms, anxiety, and regulatory problems. Overall, the literature supports sensory processing and reactivity as promising but nonspecific early markers whose predictive value is likely to increase when interpreted alongside social, attentional, motor, and regulatory indicators ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Neurocognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Temperamental style, physiological arousal, and early emotion regulation have been studied as candidate infant markers because they index how infants respond to novelty, recover from stress, and sustain organized engagement with the environment. In prospective infant-sibling cohorts, later autistic outcomes have been associated not with a single temperament profile but with elevations in negative affect, reduced approach or surgency, and difficulties regulating distress across the first year, suggesting broad perturbations in reactivity-regulation systems rather than disorder-specific signatures ref [49], ref [50].

Work linking these dimensions to emerging neurodevelopmental risk also emphasizes biological arousal. In infancy, atypical autonomic regulation, including altered parasympathetic functioning indexed by respiratory sinus arrhythmia, has been related to poorer social engagement and less adaptive regulatory behavior, consistent with models in which early differences in state regulation constrain learning opportunities during social interaction ref [51]. Complementing this, longitudinal work in infants at familial likelihood for autism has shown that parent-reported temperament trajectories can differentiate later developmental outcomes, particularly when irritability and poor soothability persist rather than resolve over time ref [52].

These signals are important but nonspecific. Similar patterns of heightened negative emotionality, dysregulated arousal, and weak self-soothing also feature prominently in pathways to ADHD and broader developmental psychopathology, limiting their diagnostic specificity in isolation ref [53]. Accordingly, temperament and regulation markers are best viewed as part of a multilevel risk profile that may enhance early identification when interpreted alongside social-attentional, sensory, and motor indicators.

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Neurocognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.content:
Sleep, feeding, and broader regulatory behaviors are among the earliest parent-observable domains studied as candidate developmental risk markers. In prospective infant-sibling cohorts, parent-reported sleep difficulties, excessive crying, and problems settling have been linked to later autism-related outcomes, suggesting that dysregulated state control may precede clearer social-communication symptoms ref [54]. Such behaviors are not specific to autism, however, and are better conceptualized as transdiagnostic indicators of atypical neurodevelopmental organization and self-regulation.

Sleep disturbance has received particular attention because it is common in both autism and ADHD and may interact with emerging attention and arousal systems. Longitudinal work in infants at familial risk has shown that shorter sleep duration and poorer sleep consolidation in the first year are associated with later autistic traits and developmental difficulties ref [55], while broader reviews indicate that sleep problems are elevated early in life and may contribute to downstream cognitive and behavioral regulation challenges ref [56]. These findings are consistent with models in which early circadian and arousal regulation difficulties shape infant learning opportunities.

Feeding and related regulatory behaviors also appear informative. Atypical feeding, including early food selectivity and oral-sensory aversion, has been repeatedly described in children who later receive autism diagnoses, with evidence that these patterns can emerge in infancy and toddlerhood ref [57]. More generally, regulatory problems spanning feeding, sleeping, and crying have been associated with elevated risk for later behavioral and emotional difficulties, including attention problems ref [58]. For early identification, these domains are therefore best treated as low-specificity but clinically valuable signals that may warrant closer developmental surveillance when they co-occur with other emerging markers.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Environmental Mechanisms Underlying Early Risk
subsections.content:
Genetic liability is substantial in both autism and ADHD, but it is distributed across many common and rare variants and expressed through partially overlapping developmental pathways. Twin and family studies consistently indicate high heritability for autism and ADHD, while also showing that familial aggregation extends to subclinical traits and broader neurodevelopmental difficulties rather than neatly bounded diagnostic categories ref [59], ref [60]. This supports a dimensional view in which early-emerging differences in social attention, activity regulation, and sensory responsivity may index inherited liability before syndromic phenotypes stabilize.

Prospective infant-sibling designs have been especially informative for autism, demonstrating elevated recurrence among younger siblings and revealing that familial risk is associated with heterogeneous developmental outcomes rather than a single trajectory ref [61]. At the genomic level, common variant studies show strong polygenic contributions to both conditions, and cross-disorder analyses indicate shared genetic influences between ADHD, autism, and other childhood psychopathologies ref [62], ref [63]. Such overlap is consistent with pleiotropic liability affecting general neurodevelopmental regulation, with later symptom profiles shaped by developmental timing and context.

At the same time, familial risk is not deterministic. Rare de novo and inherited variants can confer large effects in some children, but penetrance is variable and modified by background polygenic burden and family context ref [64]. A key implication for infancy research is that family history should be treated as an index of probabilistic liability embedded within broader multilevel mechanisms, rather than as a simple proxy for inevitable disorder.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Environmental Mechanisms Underlying Early Risk
subsections.content:
Prenatal and perinatal factors are best understood as probabilistic modifiers of neurodevelopmental trajectories rather than single causal agents. Population-based studies indicate that exposure to severe maternal infection, metabolic and inflammatory conditions, and obstetric complications is associated with elevated likelihood of later autism or ADHD, although effect sizes are generally modest and likely reflect heterogeneous pathways converging on early brain development ref [65], ref [66]. This framework is consistent with models in which fetal neurodevelopment is shaped by maternal immune signaling, placental function, endocrine regulation, and nutrient availability.

Maternal immune activation has received particular attention in autism research. In a large birth cohort, elevated midgestational maternal C-reactive protein was associated with increased risk of autism in offspring, supporting links between prenatal inflammatory biology and altered neurodevelopment ref [67]. For ADHD, evidence from nationwide and sibling-comparison designs suggests that some apparent prenatal risks, such as maternal smoking during pregnancy, may be partly explained by familial confounding rather than direct teratogenic effects alone ref [68]. Such findings underscore the importance of genetically informed designs when interpreting prenatal associations.

Perinatal adversity also contributes to risk stratification. Meta-analytic evidence links prematurity, low birth weight, hypoxic-ischemic events, and other birth complications with later autism, while very preterm birth is also associated with higher rates of attentional and regulatory difficulties characteristic of ADHD ref [69], ref [70]. Overall, prenatal and perinatal exposures likely operate through transactional mechanisms: they may amplify vulnerability in genetically susceptible infants, alter early brain organization, and shape the postnatal environments into which neurodevelopment unfolds.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Environmental Mechanisms Underlying Early Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Early Brain Development and Neural Organization
subsections.content:
Early brain development is increasingly understood as a key level at which autism and ADHD liability may become biologically instantiated. Longitudinal infant neuroimaging studies suggest that altered developmental timing, rather than fixed lesion-like abnormalities, is especially relevant. In autism, infants later diagnosed with the condition show accelerated cortical surface area expansion in the first year, followed by brain overgrowth in the second year, linking early neuroanatomical divergence to emerging social-communicative symptoms ref [71]. Complementary work in high-familial-risk cohorts has also identified differences in white-matter developmental trajectories across the first two years of life, consistent with altered maturation of large-scale connectivity ref [72].

Functional organization also appears atypical early in development. Resting-state functional connectivity MRI obtained at 6 months has been shown to predict later autism diagnosis, suggesting that alterations in distributed network organization can precede overt behavioral symptoms ref [73]. More broadly, autism has been conceptualized as involving disrupted neural synchronization across cortical systems, with implications for perception, social processing, and developmental specialization ref [74]. In ADHD, structural MRI meta-analysis indicates reliable reductions in subcortical volumes and delayed maturation within frontostriatal and related circuits, supporting models of altered neural timing and executive-attentional network development rather than focal dysfunction alone ref [75].

Together, these findings support a developmental systems view in which early-emerging differences in brain growth, connectivity, and network specialization contribute to later phenotypic divergence. They also underscore that neural organization is shaped dynamically across infancy and early childhood, creating a substrate through which genetic liability and prenatal or postnatal exposures may influence later autism and ADHD outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Environmental Mechanisms Underlying Early Risk
subsections.content:
Psychophysiological and arousal systems are plausible early mechanisms linking biological liability to emerging autistic and ADHD phenotypes. In autism, atypical autonomic regulation has been interpreted as reflecting altered responsivity to social and sensory input, with evidence for elevated baseline arousal and reduced flexibility of state regulation in some infants and children, particularly in electrodermal and cardiac measures ref [76], ref [77]. Such differences may constrain attention allocation, tolerance of novelty, and the ability to coordinate engagement with caregivers during early development.

Related models in ADHD emphasize dysregulation of arousal and state control, proposing that variability in alertness and autonomic activation contributes to inattention, hyperactivity, and impaired self-regulation ref [78]. Although much of this literature derives from later childhood, infant work suggests that temperamental reactivity, vagal regulation, and difficulties modulating behavioral state may represent early indicators of developmental divergence. Across both conditions, psychophysiological markers are best viewed not as disorder-specific signatures, but as transdiagnostic dimensions that interact with sensory responsivity, executive control, and social engagement.

Importantly, arousal profiles are dynamic and context-sensitive. A transactional perspective suggests that infant autonomic regulation both shapes and is shaped by caregiver scaffolding, environmental predictability, and cumulative stress exposure. This framing is consistent with polyvagal and neurovisceral integration accounts, which link vagal control to attentional regulation, affective flexibility, and adaptive social behavior ref [79], ref [80]. Thus, early psychophysiological measures may help explain heterogeneity in developmental pathways while remaining embedded within broader multilevel models of neurodevelopmental risk.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Environmental Mechanisms Underlying Early Risk
subsections.content:
Caregiving and broader environmental context are increasingly viewed as modifiers of early neurodevelopmental trajectories rather than primary causes of autism or ADHD. Contemporary developmental models emphasize that infant social behavior emerges through repeated transactions between child characteristics and caregiver responses; thus, parental sensitivity, stress, and opportunities for contingent interaction may shape how inherited liabilities are expressed over time. In autism, prospective infant-sibling studies suggest that early parent–child interaction is often adaptive but can become strained as atypical social communication becomes more evident, supporting a transactional rather than parent-driven account of divergence ref [81].

Attachment findings broadly indicate that many autistic children form secure attachments, although rates of security may be somewhat reduced at the group level and are influenced by co-occurring cognitive and regulatory difficulties ref [82]. In ADHD, caregiving adversity and inconsistent or harsh parenting are more consistently associated with symptom severity, but genetically informed work indicates substantial bidirectional effects, with child impulsivity and inattention also eliciting more negative parenting ref [83]. These observations caution against simplistic environmental explanations while underscoring the importance of family processes as amplifiers or buffers of early risk.

Beyond dyadic caregiving, environmental context includes socioeconomic disadvantage, family stress, and exposure to deprivation or threat. Large population studies show that early psychosocial adversity is associated with elevated ADHD risk and poorer developmental outcomes, although effects are probabilistic and intertwined with familial confounding ref [84]. Reviews of early intervention further suggest that parent-mediated support can improve proximal social communication and regulatory outcomes in infants and toddlers showing emerging autistic traits, illustrating how caregiving environments may alter developmental cascades even when core etiological liability is neurobiological ref [85].

Taken together, caregiving and attachment are best conceptualized as components of a broader ecology that shapes adaptation, compensation, and symptom expression during the first years of life, operating in continuous interaction with genetic liability, neural organization, and child temperament.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Environmental Mechanisms Underlying Early Risk
subsections.content:
Gene–environment interplay in autism and ADHD is increasingly understood as transactional rather than additive. Genetic liability partly structures the environments children experience through passive and evocative gene–environment correlation, while environmental exposures can differentially affect children as a function of inherited susceptibility ref [86], ref [87]. This framework helps explain why early divergence is often probabilistic: familial liability may shape temperamental style, regulatory capacity, and caregiver responses, which then recursively influence developmental trajectories.

At the molecular level, prenatal and early postnatal environments may become biologically embedded through epigenetic regulation and stress-sensitive neurodevelopmental processes. Reviews of autism have highlighted how maternal immune activation, toxicant exposure, nutrition, and endocrine-disrupting conditions may interact with genetic vulnerability to alter synaptic development and cortical organization ref [88]. In ADHD, developmental models similarly emphasize that inherited differences in dopaminergic and executive-control systems unfold in continuous transaction with prenatal adversity, parenting, sleep, and broader social context rather than through a single causal pathway ref [89].

A neuroconstructivist perspective is especially useful in infancy because small early differences in attention, arousal, or sensory responsivity can cascade across levels of development as infants select and shape their own experiences ref [90]. Consistent with this view, transactional developmental theory argues that child characteristics and caregiving environments mutually modify one another over time, making early risk best conceptualized as a dynamic system spanning genes, brain, behavior, and context ref [91].

subsections.section_title: Longitudinal Pathways, Developmental Cascades, and Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: From Early Signs to Later Phenotypes
subsections.content:
Prospective infant studies show that early behavioral differences do not map one-to-one onto later diagnostic categories, but rather index probabilistic pathways toward a range of neurodevelopmental phenotypes. In infants later diagnosed with autism, atypicalities often emerge gradually across the first two years, including declining eye fixation to social scenes, reduced social attention, and differences in motor and communicative development rather than a single pathognomonic infancy profile ref [28], ref [92]. This developmental unfolding underscores that early signs are best understood as dynamic deviations in trajectories rather than static markers.

A similar logic applies to early liabilities relevant to ADHD. Temperamental dysregulation, elevated activity, weak attentional control, and early executive difficulties in toddlerhood and the preschool period can foreshadow later ADHD symptoms, although these pathways are neither specific nor deterministic and frequently overlap with broader regulatory and language difficulties ref [93], ref [94]. Thus, early manifestations often reflect transdiagnostic vulnerabilities that can crystallize into different later phenotypes depending on timing, co-occurring risks, and environmental context.

Longitudinal work therefore favors a developmental-cascade view in which infant social, attentional, sensory-motor, and regulatory differences transact with experience to shape later symptom profiles, impairment, and adaptive functioning. Even within elevated-likelihood cohorts, outcomes are heterogeneous: some infants with early atypicalities later meet criteria for autism or ADHD, some show subthreshold traits or other developmental difficulties, and others do not develop clinical-level syndromes ref [95], ref [96]. This heterogeneity is central to interpreting infant markers and cautions against overly linear models from early signs to later phenotype.

subsections.section_title: Longitudinal Pathways, Developmental Cascades, and Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Longitudinal work shows only partial continuity from infant risk markers to later autism or ADHD phenotypes. In autism, early social-communication atypicalities and emerging repetitive behavior can be detectable in the second year, yet trajectories vary markedly in onset, slope, and outcome, with some children showing gradual symptom consolidation and others demonstrating later-emerging difficulties or attenuation over time ref [97], ref [98]. Comparable heterogeneity is evident in ADHD-related pathways: early motor, regulatory, and attentional differences may foreshadow later symptoms, but infant predictors are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and developmental timing matters for whether difficulties crystallize into clinically significant inattention/hyperactivity ref [99].

This pattern underscores both developmental continuity and discontinuity. Diagnostic stability increases from toddlerhood onward, but early classifications are less stable than later ones, particularly near threshold presentations and in children with changing cognitive or language profiles ref [98], ref [100]. Trajectories may therefore reflect cascading transactions between neurodevelopmental liability and shifting environmental demands, such that impairments become more visible at transition points when social, executive, or adaptive expectations increase. In ADHD, longitudinal studies similarly suggest that persistence, remission, and late-emerging symptom patterns are all observed, complicating any simple infant-to-diagnosis model ref [101].

A developmental-timing perspective is therefore essential: the same early difference may have different implications depending on age, co-occurring abilities, and the maturational window in which it appears. Repeated measurement across infancy, preschool, and school entry is especially important for distinguishing transient delays from enduring pathways and for identifying periods when intervention may alter subsequent cascades ref [97], ref [100], ref [101].

subsections.section_title: Longitudinal Pathways, Developmental Cascades, and Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Comorbidity and symptom overlap are central to understanding longitudinal pathways in autism and ADHD. Epidemiologic and clinical studies show that co-occurrence is common, with substantial proportions of autistic individuals meeting criteria for ADHD and vice versa, challenging earlier diagnostic conventions that treated the conditions as mutually exclusive ref [102], ref [18]. Shared difficulties in attention regulation, inhibitory control, motor activity, and social reciprocity can complicate early phenotyping, especially when infant markers are broad indicators of neurodevelopmental atypicality rather than syndrome-specific signs.

At the symptom level, overlap does not imply equivalence. Factor-analytic and family-genetic work suggests partially separable but correlated liability dimensions, consistent with both shared and distinct mechanisms ref [103], ref [104]. In development, this means that early inattentive, regulatory, or sensory-behavioral difficulties may feed into multiple later outcomes, while social-communication differences can be amplified or masked by co-occurring ADHD features. Such interplay may contribute to diagnostic instability, delayed recognition of one condition in the presence of the other, and apparent shifts in symptom prominence over time.

Clinically, comorbidity is associated with greater impairment than either condition alone, including poorer adaptive functioning, more externalizing problems, and increased service needs ref [105], ref [106]. A developmental-cascades perspective therefore argues against studying autism and ADHD in isolation: overlap is not merely a boundary problem in classification, but a major source of heterogeneity in trajectories, prognosis, and intervention response.

subsections.section_title: Longitudinal Pathways, Developmental Cascades, and Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Sex- and gender-related variation is central to understanding longitudinal heterogeneity in autism and ADHD. Both conditions are diagnosed more often in males, but accumulating evidence suggests that this disparity reflects not only etiologic differences but also sex-linked variation in early presentation, ascertainment, and thresholds for clinical concern. In autism, females may show fewer overt restricted and repetitive behaviors, relatively stronger social imitation or compensatory strategies, and higher rates of missed or delayed identification, particularly among cognitively able children ref [107], ref [108]. Parallel concerns have been raised in ADHD, where girls are more likely to present with inattentive symptoms and less disruptive behavior, increasing the chance that difficulties are overlooked until academic or emotional demands escalate ref [109].

These patterns matter developmentally because apparent continuity or discontinuity can be shaped by who is recognized, when, and on what basis. Sex-differential trajectories may therefore reflect both biology and context, including referral biases, gendered expectations, and the interaction of symptoms with co-occurring anxiety, depression, or social stressors. Reviews of autism in girls and women emphasize that a male-typical evidence base may obscure phenotypic diversity across development ref [110], while population work in ADHD shows persistent sex differences in symptom configuration and impairment despite substantial overlap between males and females ref [111].

At the same time, sex is only one axis of individual variation. Dimensional approaches that foreground person-specific profiles—cognitive strengths and liabilities, language level, temperament, adaptive skills, and environmental supports—are essential for explaining why infants with superficially similar early signs diverge into markedly different later outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Longitudinal Pathways, Developmental Cascades, and Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Adaptive functioning provides a crucial complement to symptom-based characterization because later outcomes are shaped not only by diagnostic status, but by how children manage everyday communication, social participation, self-care, and learning demands. In autism, adaptive skills are often substantially lower than would be expected from IQ alone, and this gap can widen with age, indicating that developmental change in real-world functioning does not simply track cognitive level ref [112]. Longitudinal work further suggests marked heterogeneity: some children show gains in daily living and communication, whereas others plateau or fall further behind age expectations, underscoring the need to model trajectories rather than static endpoints ref [113].

For ADHD, broader outcomes frequently extend beyond core inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms to academic underachievement, social difficulties, accidental injury, and later occupational and mental health impairment. Follow-up studies indicate that childhood ADHD predicts persistent functional burden even when symptom profiles change over time, highlighting the importance of impairment-based outcomes in developmental models ref [114]. At the population level, ADHD is also associated with elevated risks of premature mortality, especially through accidents and other external causes, emphasizing that longitudinal pathways have major public-health significance ref [115].

Across both conditions, adaptive outcomes are strongly conditioned by co-occurring language, intellectual, emotional-behavioral, and family-context factors, rather than by diagnostic category alone. This supports a developmental-cascade perspective in which early neurodevelopmental differences interact with support access, comorbidity, and environmental demands to produce diverse adult profiles in independence, education, employment, and quality of life ref [113], ref [116].

subsections.section_title: Longitudinal Pathways, Developmental Cascades, and Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Longitudinal outcomes in autism and ADHD are shaped not only by early liability but also by the accumulation and timing of risk and protective influences. Developmental psychopathology models emphasize that neurodevelopmental symptoms unfold within broader transactional contexts, in which child characteristics, caregiving, and environmental demands can amplify or attenuate later impairment. Prospective studies indicate that elevated infant familial liability does not deterministically lead to adverse outcomes; rather, substantial variability is observed in symptom persistence, adaptive skills, and mental health, consistent with probabilistic rather than fixed pathways ref [117], ref [118].

Protective factors appear to include more efficient early regulatory capacities, stronger language and cognitive skills, and supportive, responsive caregiving environments. In autism, better early social communication and cognitive functioning have been linked to more favorable later adaptive outcomes, even when core traits remain present ref [119]. In ADHD and related externalizing pathways, sensitive parenting and reduced family adversity are associated with lower levels of later behavioral dysregulation, whereas cumulative psychosocial stress increases risk for persistent impairment and comorbidity ref [120]. These findings support cascade models in which early self-regulation and caregiver scaffolding can redirect developmental trajectories.

Resilience should therefore be understood as dynamic adaptation rather than the absence of symptoms. It may involve compensatory skill development, environmental fit, and access to timely supports, including early intervention and educational accommodation. Work on cumulative risk further suggests that multiple modest adversities can jointly erode resilience, while promotive contexts can buffer liability across development ref [121], ref [122]. A key implication is that prognosis is best framed in terms of modifiable pathways and person-environment transactions, not early symptoms alone.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to the Study of Infant Pathways to Autism and ADHD
subsections.subsection_title: Prospective Longitudinal and High-Risk Cohort Designs
subsections.content:
Prospective longitudinal designs are foundational for studying infant pathways to autism and ADHD because they characterize development before clinical symptoms are fully expressed. By repeatedly sampling behavior, physiology, and context from the first months of life, these studies reduce retrospective bias and allow investigators to examine whether early differences reflect causal liabilities, compensatory processes, or nonspecific developmental perturbations. High-risk infant-sibling cohorts have been especially influential in autism research because recurrence rates are substantially elevated in younger siblings of autistic children, making these samples efficient for tracing prodromal variation and later diagnostic outcomes ref [61], ref [123].

A major strength of high-risk cohorts is their capacity to map developmental timing. In autism, prospective sibling studies have shown that overt behavioral markers are often limited in early infancy and become clearer over the first two years, supporting a view of divergence as an emergent process rather than a fixed neonatal phenotype ref [124]. Analogous logic has guided infant studies of ADHD liability, including work following children with familial risk or elevated early regulatory and attentional difficulties to identify precursors of later symptom dimensions ref [125]. Such designs are also well suited to testing cross-syndrome continuity and overlap, which is critical given shared familial and genetic liability across neurodevelopmental conditions.

However, these cohorts also have important limitations. Familial-risk samples may not generalize to simplex cases or to community pathways shaped by socioeconomic adversity, prematurity, or environmental exposures. Attrition, shifting diagnostic criteria, and outcome heterogeneity further complicate inference, while enrichment for multiplex families can inflate estimates of predictive utility. Recent large consortia and multisite studies have addressed some of these issues by increasing sample size, harmonizing protocols, and incorporating broader phenotyping, but the field still faces a central challenge: balancing etiologic enrichment against representativeness when drawing conclusions about early developmental risk ref [126], ref [127].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to the Study of Infant Pathways to Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
Behavioral observation and standardized assessment remain central for characterizing infant pathways to autism and ADHD because they capture the phenotypic expressions most proximal to everyday functioning. In prospective studies, direct observation of social attention, motor behavior, affect regulation, and emerging executive control can reveal subtle deviations before syndromic presentations are clinically obvious. Repeated assessments are particularly informative, as early risk is often expressed through altered developmental trajectories rather than stable deficits at a single age point.

For autism, structured observational tools and dimensional coding of infant behavior have been especially influential. Longitudinal work in high-risk infant siblings showed that behavioral markers are often limited at 6 months but become more discriminative in the second year, underscoring the value of repeated standardized observation rather than one-time screening ref [128], ref [129]. Measures such as the Autism Observation Scale for Infants were developed to systematize early behavioral signs, though their utility is strongest when embedded within broader developmental follow-up rather than treated as stand-alone diagnostic instruments ref [130].

For ADHD-related pathways, infant assessment has relied more heavily on broad measures of temperament, activity level, attentional regulation, and early executive functions, because disorder-specific instruments for infancy are less established. Parent-report scales can efficiently sample behavior across contexts, but they are vulnerable to expectancy and contrast effects, especially in enriched-risk cohorts. Laboratory paradigms add experimental control yet may have limited ecological validity and modest cross-task convergence. Across both conditions, the major methodological challenge is that infant behavior is heterogeneous, state-dependent, and developmentally transient, making multimethod assessment and longitudinal replication essential for distinguishing transient variation from clinically meaningful risk ref [131], ref [132].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to the Study of Infant Pathways to Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
Neurophysiological and neuroimaging methods are central to infant pathways research because they can index emerging atypical development before behavioral symptoms are clinically obvious. Electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potentials are especially valuable in infancy due to their temporal resolution, relative tolerability, and feasibility in repeated longitudinal designs. In infants later diagnosed with autism, altered responses to faces, gaze, and social cues have been reported in the first years of life, suggesting divergence in perceptual and attentional processing rather than a single early biomarker ref [133], ref [134]. Resting and task-related EEG has also been used to study early regulatory and attentional processes relevant to later ADHD, although findings are often less specific and may reflect broader liability for neurodevelopmental difficulties.

Structural and functional neuroimaging adds complementary information about large-scale brain development. Magnetic resonance imaging studies in high-risk infant sibling cohorts have linked later autism outcomes to altered trajectories of cortical surface area expansion and brain volume growth across the first two years of life ref [71]. Functional connectivity MRI has similarly identified atypical patterns of network organization in early infancy that improve prediction of later diagnosis at the group level ref [135]. Such work supports the view that risk is expressed in distributed neural systems and developmental timing, not solely in isolated regions or modalities.

Methodologically, these measures are powerful but challenging. Infant EEG and MRI are vulnerable to motion, sleep state, variable attention, and small usable sample sizes after artifact rejection. Cross-site harmonization, preregistration, and multimodal integration with behavior and family-risk data are therefore critical. Importantly, prospective infant neuroimaging has yielded more robust findings for autism than for ADHD to date, underscoring the need for larger transdiagnostic cohorts and repeated measurement designs that can distinguish general developmental perturbation from pathway-specific risk ref [136], ref [137].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to the Study of Infant Pathways to Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
Measurement in infancy is constrained by rapid developmental change, state dependence, and limited behavioral repertoire. The same behavior may reflect different underlying processes at 3, 9, or 18 months, making construct validity and age-equivalence difficult to establish. In addition, infant performance varies with arousal, feeding, sleep, and caregiver context, which can attenuate reliability and obscure group differences. These problems are especially salient in research on emerging autism and ADHD, where effect sizes are often small and trajectories are more informative than single time points ref [138], ref [139].

A central challenge is that commonly used instruments were designed for broad developmental surveillance rather than fine-grained characterization of neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Standardized tests may show floor effects, limited sensitivity to atypical developmental pathways, and poor comparability across waves because forms and item content change with age. Parent-report measures add important ecological information but are vulnerable to shared-method variance and differences in parental interpretation, particularly in high-risk family studies ref [140], ref [130].

These limitations motivate repeated, multimethod measurement and explicit psychometric evaluation. Recommendations from developmental methodology emphasize testing measurement invariance, modeling within-person change, and combining observational, physiological, and caregiver-report indicators rather than treating any single measure as definitive. Work on reproducibility in infant research further highlights the need for larger samples, harmonized protocols, and transparent handling of missingness and attrition, which are endemic in infant cohorts ref [141], ref [142].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to the Study of Infant Pathways to Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
Data integration and predictive modeling are increasingly central to infant studies of later autism and ADHD because single measures rarely provide sufficient sensitivity or specificity at the individual level. Multimodal designs combine behavioral observation, eye tracking, EEG, MRI, family-history information, and developmental assessments to capture distributed and time-varying risk signals across infancy. This strategy is especially well suited to neurodevelopmental conditions characterized by heterogeneity, developmental change, and overlapping phenotypes.

In autism research, work from prospective infant-sibling cohorts has shown that prediction improves when features are aggregated across domains and timepoints rather than treated as isolated markers. For example, machine-learning analyses of structural MRI in high-risk infants achieved substantial accuracy in predicting later autism diagnosis, illustrating the promise of multivariate approaches while also underscoring the need for independent validation ref [71]. Related work integrating multiple behavioral and biological measures has emphasized that no single early feature is determinative; instead, probabilistic risk is distributed across partially redundant indicators ref [143], ref [144]. Parallel arguments have emerged in developmental psychopathology more broadly, where multivariate models are framed as tools for parsing equifinality and developmental heterogeneity rather than simply maximizing classification performance ref [145].

Methodologically, the main challenges are small samples relative to feature space, missing data, site and instrument effects, and outcome labels that may change with age. Best practice therefore requires rigorous cross-validation, transparent feature selection, calibration assessment, and, crucially, external replication before clinical translation. Recent large-scale initiatives combining EEG and MRI across infant cohorts highlight both the feasibility and difficulty of building generalizable predictive models from early neurodevelopmental data ref [146].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to the Study of Infant Pathways to Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
A central limitation of infant pathway research is that many cohorts are recruited through familial-likelihood designs, often enrolling siblings of autistic children or children selected for elevated ADHD risk. These designs are powerful for prospective characterization of early emergence, but they do not constitute population-representative samples and may overrepresent families with greater clinical awareness, research access, and willingness to participate. As a result, estimates of prevalence, developmental timing, and marker performance may not generalize straightforwardly to community populations or to infants whose risk arises through non-familial pathways ref [147], ref [148].

Generalizability is further constrained by persistent sociodemographic skew. Developmental cognitive neuroscience samples are disproportionately drawn from White, higher-income, and highly educated families, limiting inference about how early behavior and brain measures operate across contexts of structural inequality. Reviews of infant neuroimaging and developmental science have highlighted underreporting of race, ethnicity, language background, and socioeconomic indicators, alongside systematic barriers to participation that can shape both attrition and apparent developmental norms ref [149], ref [150]. In autism specifically, delayed or unequal identification across racialized and marginalized groups underscores the risk of building early markers on already biased ascertainment pipelines ref [151].

Improving sampling therefore requires more than demographic description. Community-based recruitment, multilingual and culturally adapted assessments, flexible visit structures, and analytic attention to selection and attrition bias are necessary to test transportability of findings. Frameworks for inclusive developmental science emphasize that heterogeneity should be modeled rather than treated as nuisance variance, particularly when studying conditions such as autism and ADHD whose developmental expression is likely modified by social context, healthcare access, and exposure to adversity ref [150], ref [152].

references

subsections.section_title: Early Identification, Intervention, and Translational Implications
subsections.content:
Screening and early detection strategies increasingly draw on prospective infant studies to identify behavioral risk markers before the age at which autism or ADHD are typically diagnosed. For autism, population screening in the second year of life is now feasible, with instruments such as the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers showing utility when embedded in pediatric surveillance, although performance improves when combined with follow-up interview and developmental monitoring rather than treated as a stand-alone diagnostic filter [1]. In parallel, observational tools targeting social communication in the first 18 months, including the First Year Inventory, have been developed to extend detection closer to infancy, but these measures remain better suited to risk enrichment than definitive prediction [2].

For ADHD, screening in infancy is more challenging because cardinal symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity are developmentally diffuse early in life. Current approaches therefore emphasize repeated surveillance of temperamental regulation, activity level, and emerging executive-control difficulties, often in conjunction with family history and broader neurodevelopmental concerns [3]. Across both conditions, multistage strategies that combine parent report, clinician observation, and longitudinal reassessment are likely to outperform one-time screens, particularly in high-likelihood groups such as younger siblings of autistic children, where early atypicalities in attention, social engagement, and motor development can already be quantified [4].

A key translational implication is that screening should be framed as probabilistic and developmentally dynamic. Even well-validated tools generate false positives and false negatives, and symptom trajectories may diverge substantially across infancy and toddlerhood. Accordingly, recent diagnostic frameworks for autism emphasize early developmental history, repeated clinical judgment, and the integration of dimensional information rather than reliance on any single infant marker [5].

subsections.section_title: Early Identification, Intervention, and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in Prediction and Clinical Utility
subsections.content:
A central translational challenge is that group-level markers of later autism or ADHD rarely provide sufficiently precise prediction for individual infants. Elevated-likelihood cohorts have revealed early differences in attention, social communication, motor development, and brain measures, but effect sizes are often modest, trajectories are heterogeneous, and many infants showing early atypicalities do not go on to meet diagnostic criteria, whereas others who are later diagnosed show little early deviation on available measures ref [158], ref [159]. This limits positive predictive value, especially when tools are extended from enriched research samples to general population settings.

Clinical utility is further constrained by developmental instability and overlap across neurodevelopmental outcomes. Dimensional traits associated with autism and ADHD co-occur with broader language, motor, and regulatory difficulties, making it difficult to determine whether infant markers index disorder-specific risk, general neurodevelopmental vulnerability, or transient variation ref [160], ref [161]. Reviews of early ASD screening also note that performance depends strongly on age, sampling frame, and follow-up interval, underscoring that sensitivity and specificity are not fixed properties of a measure but of the context in which it is used ref [162].

Accordingly, translational value may lie less in deterministic prediction than in stratifying need for monitoring and support. Recent work on large-scale developmental surveillance for autism and ADHD emphasizes combining repeated measurement, family history, and multi-domain indicators while communicating uncertainty transparently to families and clinicians ref [163]. Such approaches may better balance the promise of earlier identification against the risks of over-referral, false reassurance, and premature labeling.

subsections.section_title: Early Identification, Intervention, and Translational Implications
subsections.content:
Parent-mediated interventions are especially attractive in infancy because they can be embedded in everyday routines, capitalize on high caregiver contact, and target emerging social-communicative processes before more entrenched difficulties appear. Across autism-focused work, these approaches typically aim to increase parental sensitivity and contingency, scaffold attention and reciprocity, and create developmentally appropriate opportunities for shared engagement rather than teaching isolated skills. Trials of pre-emptive intervention in infants showing early behavioural signs or familial likelihood have shown that modifying parent–infant interaction is feasible and can shift proximal developmental processes, even when effects on later diagnosis are more variable ref [164], ref [165].

Developmentally informed models emphasize that intervention targets should match the infant’s current capacities and the mechanisms thought to organize later symptoms. For autism, this has motivated interventions focused on attention to social partners, imitation, turn-taking, and dyadic synchrony; for example, caregiver-mediated programs such as iBASIS-VIPP have reported improvements in parent–child social communication and, in some studies, reductions in later autism symptom severity ref [165], ref [166]. Broader naturalistic developmental behavioral interventions similarly rest on the premise that learning is optimized when social motivation, affect regulation, and communication are supported within reciprocal play and daily activities ref [167].

For ADHD-related risk, the translational evidence base in infancy is less mature, but adjacent developmental research suggests that parent training targeting co-regulation, responsiveness, and early executive/attentional support may be a plausible preventive pathway. Existing early parenting interventions for infants at elevated neurodevelopmental risk indicate that benefits are most likely when supports are individualized, low-burden, and responsive to family stress and infant temperament ref [168], ref [169]. Overall, parent-mediated intervention is promising not because it eliminates uncertainty, but because it offers a mechanism-focused and family-centered way to support development during a period of high plasticity.

subsections.section_title: Early Identification, Intervention, and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Timing and Targets of Preventive Approaches
subsections.content:
A central translational question is not only whether infant markers predict later autism or ADHD, but when intervention is most likely to alter developmental course. Prospective work suggests that the first two years are characterized by cascading changes in attention, social engagement, motor control, and regulatory function, implying that preventive approaches may be most effective when they target emerging developmental processes rather than later-emerging diagnostic symptoms. In autism, atypical trajectories in visual attention and social communication appear to consolidate across the first year and into toddlerhood, supporting a rationale for intervention during periods of high neural and behavioral plasticity rather than waiting for diagnostic certainty ref [28], ref [170].

This timing argument has shaped trials that begin in infancy or the prodromal toddler period. Parent-mediated models such as iBASIS-VIPP aim to modify reciprocal interaction and infant attentional engagement before full syndrome expression; follow-up from a randomized trial suggested reduced autism symptom severity over time, while also underscoring that effects are probabilistic and developmentally mediated rather than curative ref [165]. More broadly, developmental intervention studies in very young autistic children indicate that gains are most plausible when targets are proximal, malleable, and embedded in everyday routines, including social orienting, joint engagement, play, and caregiver responsiveness ref [171].

For ADHD, the preventive window may partly center on infancy and preschool periods when executive attention, activity regulation, sleep, and parent-child coercive cycles are becoming organized. Because early risk is heterogeneous and often nonspecific, intervention targets may be better defined at the level of transdiagnostic mechanisms—self-regulation, arousal modulation, language, and family interaction—than at the level of categorical disorder prevention. This perspective is consistent with developmental accounts arguing that early intervention should align with mechanism-rich pathways while avoiding overpromising disorder-specific prevention in the face of substantial equifinality and shifting phenotype across childhood ref [172], ref [173].

subsections.section_title: Early Identification, Intervention, and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Family Support and Communication of Risk
subsections.content:
Communicating elevated likelihood for autism or ADHD in infancy requires balancing transparency with uncertainty. Because most infant markers confer probabilistic rather than deterministic risk, clinicians should avoid conveying early differences as a diagnosis-in-waiting and instead frame findings in terms of developmental monitoring, support options, and the wide range of possible outcomes. Work on parental experiences in prospective infant-sibling studies shows that families value clear explanations, opportunities to ask questions, and guidance that links risk information to actionable next steps rather than to passive surveillance alone ref [174], ref [175].

Family support is also shaped by the emotional consequences of risk communication. Parents of infants at familial likelihood for autism often report heightened vigilance, anxiety, and uncertainty, but also a desire for practical strategies that can be embedded in everyday interactions. A family-centered approach therefore emphasizes validation of parental concerns, shared decision-making, and attention to the broader caregiving context, including parental mental health and stress. Such priorities are consistent with policy and clinical guidance that recommends developmental surveillance as an ongoing partnership with families rather than a one-time disclosure event ref [176], ref [177].

Importantly, communication of risk should be culturally sensitive and responsive to differences in health literacy, service access, and prior experiences with neurodevelopmental conditions. Emerging intervention work further suggests that when concerns are paired with supportive coaching and strengths-based messaging, families are more likely to engage with early, developmentally informed support without experiencing communication as stigmatizing or fatalistic ref [178]. Translational efforts should therefore evaluate not only predictive accuracy, but also how risk information is understood, remembered, and used by families over time.

subsections.section_title: Early Identification, Intervention, and Translational Implications
subsections.content:
A central priority for translational research is to move beyond single early markers toward developmentally sensitive, multilevel prediction models that integrate behavior, family history, neural measures, and environmental context. Prospective infant-sibling studies have demonstrated both the promise and the limits of early prediction, showing substantial heterogeneity in developmental trajectories and outcomes, which cautions against deterministic interpretations of early risk signals ref [136], ref [179]. Future work will therefore need larger, more diverse longitudinal cohorts and explicit tests of transportability across clinics, community settings, and sociodemographic groups.

A second direction is to embed mechanistic and intervention science more tightly together. Rather than asking only whether infants can be classified early, translational studies should identify malleable developmental processes and test whether changing caregiver-infant interaction, attention regulation, or sensory engagement alters later outcomes. Emerging trials of preemptive, parent-mediated approaches illustrate this shift toward developmental targets that are actionable before full syndrome expression ref [180]. Linking such trials to repeated measurement of candidate mechanisms could clarify for whom, when, and how early support is beneficial.

Finally, translational progress will depend on frameworks that prioritize clinical utility, equity, and responsible implementation. Reviews of early autism detection have emphasized that screening tools must be evaluated not only for accuracy but also for feasibility, acceptability, and consequences for families and services ref [181]. At the same time, developmental models of neurodivergence argue for outcomes that extend beyond symptom reduction to include adaptation, participation, and family well-being ref [182]. These priorities are especially important as infancy research is extended to ADHD, where predictive validity remains more limited and translational claims should remain proportionate to current evidence.
